hypotheses.title: SingleProviderHelper._calculateOutputLPAndProtocolFee missing overflow check on unchecked addition
hypotheses.description: SingleProviderHelper._calculateOutputLPAndProtocolFee (line 170-171) performs `unchecked { amountInAfterFees = reserveAmountIn + lpFeeAmount; }` without any overflow guard. The identical function in FixedHelper (lines 1067-1072) includes an explicit check: `if (amountInAfterFees < lpFeeAmount) { revert FixedPool__Overflow(); }`. When sqrtPriceX96 is near MIN_SQRT_RATIO (~2^32) and amountOut is ~2^127 (max uint128 reserve), calculateFixedOutput returns reserveAmountIn ~2^255. With poolFeeBPS >= 5001, lpFeeAmount = mulDivRoundingUp(2^255, 5001, 4999) > 2^255, and their sum overflows uint256. The wrapped amountInAfterFees becomes near-zero, making the swap appear to cost almost nothing for full reserves. The AMM's _validateProtocolFees (line 1662) catches this downstream because totalFees > wrapped amountIn always holds when overflow occurs, but SingleProviderHelper itself silently produces corrupted values — a defense-in-depth gap exploitable if AMM validation is ever relaxed or bypassed.

grounded_in.description: unchecked { amountInAfterFees = reserveAmountIn + lpFeeAmount; } — no overflow check
Same pattern but WITH overflow guard: if (amountInAfterFees < lpFeeAmount) revert FixedPool__Overflow()
Downstream guard: if (totalFees > amountIn) revert — catches corrupted amountIn from overflow

hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. SingleProvider pool with hook returning sqrtPriceX96 near MIN_SQRT_RATIO (4295128739). 2. Pool has ~2^127 output token reserves, poolFeeBPS = 5001. 3. Attacker calls swapByOutput for full reserves. 4. calculateFixedOutput returns reserveAmountIn ~2^255. 5. lpFeeAmount = mulDivRoundingUp(2^255, 5001, 4999) ~= 2^255.0003. 6. unchecked sum overflows uint256, wrapping to near-zero. 7. AMM's _validateProtocolFees catches it (totalFees > wrapped amountIn), but SingleProviderHelper returns corrupted state.

hypotheses.title: FixedHelper.collectFees compounds four independent Q128 truncations, systematically losing LP fees
hypotheses.description: FixedHelper.collectFees (lines 577-580) calculates fee0 and fee1 by performing four independent integer divisions by Q128: `fee0 = (growthA - lastA) / Q128 + (growthB - lastB) / Q128` and same for fee1. Each division truncates up to Q128-1 units (~3.4e38 in the X128 domain). With four independent divisions, a position collecting small fees loses up to 4*(Q128-1) X128-units per collection event. A single `(sum_of_growth_deltas) / Q128` would lose at most Q128-1 total, meaning the current implementation loses up to 4x more. For 18-decimal tokens, each truncation event loses up to 1 wei. Over 1000 fee collections across many positions, this creates ~4000 wei of permanently locked dust per token. The locked fees remain in the pool's fee accounting system (tracked in feeBalance0/feeBalance1 at AMMModule lines 1438/1442) but are never distributable to any LP.

grounded_in.description: fee0 = (feeGrowthInside0Of0X128 - position.feeGrowthInside0Of0LastX128) / Q128 + (feeGrowthInside0Of1X128 - position.feeGrowthInside0Of1LastX128) / Q128; fee1 similarly — four independent Q128 divisions

hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. Fixed pool with 100 active positions across multiple height intervals, ratio 1:1. 2. 10,000 small swaps each generating small fee events (feeGrowthDelta < Q128 per component). 3. Each position calls collectFees: 4 divisions * (Q128-1) max truncation each = 4 wei worst case per collection. 4. 100 positions * 100 collection events = 10,000 collections. 5. Cumulative locked dust: up to 40,000 wei for 18-decimal tokens. 6. These tokens are tracked in AMM feeBalance but never claimable by any LP position.

hypotheses.title: FixedHelper._increaseHeight unchecked consumedLiquidity addition has no overflow guard unlike _decreaseHeight
hypotheses.description: FixedHelper._increaseHeight (line 1866) uses `unchecked { height.consumedLiquidity += amount; }` to track total liquidity consumed on a height side. Unlike _decreaseHeight (lines 1763-1767) which has an explicit `if (height.consumedLiquidity < amount) revert FixedPool__UnderflowConsumedLiquidity()` underflow check, _increaseHeight has NO overflow guard. If consumedLiquidity were to wrap via overflow, the height system's fundamental invariant breaks: `updateExpectedReserve` (line 1365) computes expected reserves from consumedLiquidity, and a wrapped-to-zero value would make the pool appear to have full reserves when they're actually depleted. While achieving uint256 overflow requires cumulative swaps consuming ~2^256 units (practically infeasible at current gas costs), the asymmetric safety between the increase/decrease paths represents a defensive gap. The _decreaseHeight function's author clearly considered arithmetic safety necessary — the same reasoning applies to _increaseHeight.

grounded_in.description: unchecked { height.consumedLiquidity += amount; } — no overflow check in _increaseHeight
_decreaseHeight HAS underflow check: if (height.consumedLiquidity < amount) revert FixedPool__UnderflowConsumedLiquidity()

hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. Fixed pool with very small height precision (precision=1). 2. Automated high-frequency swaps consume liquidity in small increments on one height side. 3. Over extreme time, consumedLiquidity approaches uint256.max. 4. Next _increaseHeight wraps consumedLiquidity to near-zero. 5. updateExpectedReserve computes expectedReserve as if almost no liquidity consumed, enabling LPs to withdraw more than deposited. 6. Practically infeasible at current EVM gas costs (~2^256 units) but is an asymmetric safety gap.

hypotheses.title: SingleProviderPoolType reads stale reserves via VIEW call before hook price query, enabling reserve/price desync
hypotheses.description: SingleProviderPoolType.swapByInput (line 312) and swapByOutput (line 397) read pool reserves via `ILimitBreakAMM(AMM).getPoolState(poolId)` as a VIEW call BEFORE querying the pool hook for the swap price via `getPoolPriceForSwap` (lines 323-326 / 408-412). The reserve value (used to cap output at swapCache.reserveOut) reflects state at the moment of the VIEW call. If the pool hook's getPoolPriceForSwap callback has side effects or triggers state changes that modify reserves (e.g., via composable hooks that atomically adjust positions), the swap operates on stale reserve data. The AMM's _safeDecrementUint128 at lines 1437/1440 would catch reserve underflow, preventing actual token theft. However, the stale read creates a window where the pool type approves amountOut based on higher-than-actual reserves and a price chosen by the hook with knowledge that reserves have changed. This is particularly relevant because SingleProviderPoolType.swapByInput's fallback (line 43: `if amountOut > swapCache.reserveOut`) uses the stale reserveOut as the cap for the fallback output amount.

grounded_in.description: PoolState memory poolState = ILimitBreakAMM(AMM).getPoolState(poolId); — reads reserves BEFORE hook price query
sqrtPriceCurrentX96 = ISingleProviderPoolHook(poolHook).getPoolPriceForSwap(...); — hook called AFTER reserve read
Same pattern in swapByOutput: getPoolState called before getPoolPriceForSwap

hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. Malicious pool hook implements getPoolPriceForSwap to detect swap context and trigger a composable operation modifying the pool's reserves (e.g., removing liquidity from the pool). 2. SingleProviderPoolType already cached the OLD (higher) reserve at line 312. 3. Hook returns a price that, combined with stale higher reserves, allows a larger amountOut than actual reserves support. 4. AMM's _safeDecrementUint128 catches actual reserve underflow, but the stale read enables the hook to manipulate effective price-reserve combinations not possible with fresh data.

hypotheses.title: SingleProviderHelper swapByInput-to-swapByOutput fallback recalculates fees with different formula, creating directional rounding bias
hypotheses.description: SingleProviderHelper.swapByInput (lines 29-56) has a fallback path: when calculated output exceeds reserveOut, it delegates to swapByOutput with amountOut=reserveOut (line 47). The two paths compute fees differently: swapByInput uses _calculateInputLPAndProtocolFee (fee = ceil(amountIn * feeBPS / MAX_BPS)), while the fallback's swapByOutput uses _calculateOutputLPAndProtocolFee (fee = ceil(reserveAmountIn * feeBPS / (MAX_BPS - feeBPS))). For the same economic trade, these formulas are mathematically equivalent but round independently via separate mulDivRoundingUp operations. The input path already computed and DISCARDED its fee calculation (lines 33-37); the output fallback recomputes from scratch. The two paths can produce fee values differing by 1-2 wei. Since the fallback fee formula is applied on the smaller base (reserveAmountIn < amountIn), and uses (MAX_BPS - feeBPS) as denominator, it tends to produce slightly different fees. Over many swaps hitting the fallback (common when pool is near reserve depletion), these discrepancies accumulate in one direction, creating a systematic bias in LP fee collection.

grounded_in.description: Fallback: if amountOut > reserveOut, set amountOut=reserveOut and delegate to swapByOutput — fees recalculated from scratch

hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. SingleProvider pool near reserve depletion (reserveOut = 100e18). 2. Swapper sends amountIn such that calculateFixedInput(amountIn - inputFee) = 100e18 + 1 (triggers fallback). 3. Fallback: swapByOutput with amountOut=100e18. Computes reserveAmountIn=calculateFixedOutput(100e18, price), then outputFee=ceil(reserveAmountIn * feeBPS / (MAX_BPS - feeBPS)). 4. Due to independent rounding, outputFee differs from inputFee by 1-2 wei. 5. Over 10,000 fallback swaps on a depleting pool, cumulative drift = ~10,000-20,000 wei in fee accounting.

hypotheses.title: FixedHelper._crossHeight fee growth outside flip under rapid height oscillation shifts fee attribution between LP positions
hypotheses.description: FixedHelper._crossHeight (lines 2016-2019) performs the Uniswap V3-style fee growth outside flip: `specificHeightInfo.feeGrowthOutside0X128 = heightCache.feeGrowthGlobalOf0X128 - specificHeightInfo.feeGrowthOutside0X128`. This relies on modular uint256 arithmetic — crossing the same height boundary twice with no fee accrual in between restores the original value. However, when a height boundary is crossed and uncrossed in rapid succession (small swaps oscillating around a boundary), and fee growth globals increase BETWEEN the two crosses (from the swap fees themselves), the flip captures the inter-cross fee growth in the feeGrowthOutside value. For positions spanning exactly one side of the oscillated height, `getFeeGrowthInside` will attribute fees from the oscillation period differently depending on position boundaries. An attacker could sandwich-oscillate a height boundary to systematically shift fee growth attribution from positions on one side to positions on the other side, holding a position on the benefiting side to extract fees rightfully belonging to other LPs.

grounded_in.description: _crossHeight flips feeGrowthOutside via subtraction from global: feeGrowthOutside = feeGrowthGlobal - feeGrowthOutside
_increaseHeight: while loop calls _crossHeight when reaching height boundaries during swap

hypotheses.exploit_scenario: 1. Fixed pool with two LPs: Alice (heights 100-200) and Bob (heights 200-300). Height boundary at 200 is oscillation target. 2. Attacker executes small zeroForOne swap (consuming through height 200 into 201), crossing the boundary. feeGrowthOutside at height 200 is flipped. 3. Fees from this swap increase feeGrowthGlobal. 4. Attacker immediately executes reverse swap (oneForZero back below 200), uncrossing the boundary. feeGrowthOutside flips again, but now captures the fee growth delta between the two crosses. 5. Net effect: fee attribution shifts — fees generated during the oscillation are attributed to positions on the side determined by the flip direction. 6. Attacker holds a position on the benefiting side, collecting fees that should have been distributed to other LPs.
